setups.trigger: Day before an event: a massive buying candle, then the next open drops off a cliff — a bearish engulfing on the 30-minute — but holds the trendline support. glossary.plain: Profit and loss — the running gain or loss on your open position that the broker app shows in dollars.
glossary.said: he's watching his P&L instead of the chart

glossary.plain: Price target. The level where you planned to take profit (or accept the loss) before you entered.
glossary.said: not going to your account until it hits your PT

glossary.plain: The monthly US jobs report, released at 8:30am ET on the first Friday of the month. The biggest scheduled data point of the week and a classic binary event.
glossary.said: tomorrow is NFP. So non-farm payrolls

glossary.plain: A scheduled event you can't control and can't trade through overnight — NFP, earnings, a Fed rate decision. The outcome is one way or the other and the gap happens while you're asleep.
glossary.said: things you can't control

glossary.plain: Borrowing cheaply in yen to buy US assets. When the dollar weakens against the yen the trade unwinds and US stocks get sold; when the dollar strengthens against the yen, stocks are fine.
glossary.said: if we have a bad yen carry trade, then guess what? The market's going to take it down

glossary.plain: The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond. His proxy for the cost of capital and for mortgage rates. Rising = bad for stocks; under 5% = still OK by his rule.
glossary.said: it's the proxy for mortgages

glossary.plain: The bond market pricing in that money will be needed for longer and in larger amounts — here, the capex for the AI/power buildout — which pushes long-term yields up.
glossary.said: they're pricing in what we call duration risk

glossary.plain: Capital expenditure — big money companies spend building things. The AI and power-grid buildout is capex, and it competes for the same borrowed money that funds stocks.
glossary.said: more capex needed, like capital expenditure

glossary.plain: Hundredths of a percent. 10 basis points = 0.10%. A 10-year move from 4.67 to 4.77 is ten basis points.
glossary.said: 10 basis points in capital on a $40 trillion debt is massive

glossary.plain: The point where the cost of debt and the return on capex meet — after which higher rates stop being survivable for asset prices. His rough marker: over 4.7.
glossary.said: when they merge or hit, which is what we call an inflection point

glossary.plain: His three easy catalysts: the 10-year yield (capital), crude oil (transportation), USD/JPY (currency). Check all three before the chart.
glossary.said: cost of capital, cost of transportation, cost of currency

glossary.plain: A sharp move one way that pulls people in, followed by a reversal that takes them out. The buy-into-the-event candle followed by the cliff open.
glossary.said: this is called a whipsaw, and this is how people get taken out

glossary.plain: A gap against the prior day's move that then holds — here TSLA gapping up over the previous day's bearish engulfing candle and never coming back below it.
glossary.said: it's a gap reversal and that's like a key, a real big key thing

insights.title: The chart dictates price. The account only dictates fear.
insights.body: Josh exited QQQ at 713 because the app said he needed 716 to break even and was down $50; the chart then hit 716. The P&L is a number about you; the chart is a number about the market. He admits he would freak out too, which is exactly why he doesn't look.
insights.said: the chart is what dictates price

insights.title: You got the sentiment right. You lost on the entry.
insights.body: Josh correctly read a bullish day (yen down, dollar strong) and still lost money, because he took the trade before the reclaim (768) and the next level (771) instead of at them. Direction is half the trade; the level is the other half, and it was given in the chat.
insights.said: you got the market sentiment right today, which is good. But the thing you're missing is the entry point

insights.title: Three things move markets: cost of capital, earnings, and the cycle.
insights.body: The robots price stocks off the cost of money. When the 10-year rises they sell a slice of the market whether or not the chart looks bullish. So his pre-chart check is three prices — the 10-year, crude, USD/JPY — because they tell him what the algorithms will do to his chart.
insights.said: markets themselves are driven by three things. Cost of capital, earnings of the company, and then the trend or market cycle

insights.title: Policy pays; politics doesn't.
insights.body: He knew in 2024 which candidate would win because he knew which one would fund the power-grid expansion, and that capex was coming either way. Real money follows policy because policy is the paycheck. That is also why the electrical-grid attack matters: it forces capex, which raises rates.
insights.said: they don't care anything about politics. They care about policy

insights.title: A bullish pattern can still be a short.
insights.body: TSLA's triangle is a bullish structure, and he is short it. Not because the pattern is wrong — because it's at resistance, into moving averages, up 7%, late in the day, ahead of NFP, with rates rising. Five reasons beat one pattern. The pattern tells you where; the catalysts tell you when.
insights.said: I'm short for a reason, not because this isn't a bullish pattern

insights.title: Trading is taking someone else's pay. Get your head right for that before the open.
insights.body: Money is one of three things people fight over, so the market will make you emotional by design. His answer is physical: cardio while reading the market, so he shows up as a treasure hunter looking for opportunity rather than someone afraid of losing. The mindset is set before 9:30, not during the trade.
insights.said: I'm literally going in and extracting somebody else's pay

insights.title: 73% is the job. Perfection is the wrong business.
insights.body: He airballs 27% of the time and calls that professional. The people who need to be right every time leave. Josh's fear after the hero trade is a perfection problem — one loss became three days off the desk.

insights.title: The best trade is often no trade.
insights.body: Find an excuse not to do anything. Friday's box is $3 wide, so the plan is to wait for the market to leave the box before touching it. Then, once in, stick with the conviction the homework earned.
insights.said: the cool thing about trading is you need to find an excuse not to do anything

insights.title: Homework is where confidence comes from — before the trade, not during.
insights.body: Every piece of his short (resistance, event, extension, time of day, rates) was known before he clicked. That's why he can ignore the noise while it works. Like a speaker who knows the material: pinpoint. If you don't know what you're talking about, the crowd — and your account — gets up and leaves.
insights.said: do your homework and you have confidence

insights.title: With a small account, risk management is not swinging.
insights.body: He said it plainly: the account is too small for real position-level risk control yet. The substitute is time — you only ask 'am I right today?', you don't hold, and you don't fight binary events. That is the risk framework until the account grows.
insights.said: your risk management is going to be on the fact that you're not swinging trades
